lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- English on Your CV
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Cauê de França | Lesson 10 -- English on Your CV
lesson.grammar_point: reporting passive and passive in recruitment texts: it is said / believed / expected that ...; candidates are expected to ...; he is said to have worked ...; CVs are screened by software
phases: The Words of the Job Market

listenings.text: People imagine that I read every CV carefully. I wish I could. For most positions, we receive hundreds of applications. So first, the CVs are screened by software. It looks for the words in the job posting. If the posting says advanced English and your CV doesn't mention English at all, you're out, even if you speak it perfectly. The ones that make it through come to me, and honestly, I spend about thirty seconds on each one at first. And here's a little secret. When a candidate says fluent, I call them, and I start the conversation in English, without warning. It's amazing how many people panic.

The biggest mistake I see on CVs is the word fluent. Everybody is fluent, apparently. Then they get to the interview, and the recruiter discovers the truth in two minutes. My advice is to be honest and specific. Describe each skill separately. Proficient in reading and writing. Brushing up on spoken English. Then add proof: a certificate, a project you did in English, a client you worked with. It is often said that honesty is a soft skill, and in recruitment it really is. The interview will show the truth anyway. And recruiters trust candidates who know their own level.

My team is spread across four countries, so everybody works in English. When a CV gets to me, I look at the track record first. Not the adjectives, the facts. What did you actually do? Then, in the interview, I'm looking for soft skills. And the one I value most is surprisingly simple. Can you say I don't know, and then ask a good question? People who can do that in a second language are gold. And about accents, I'm often asked if a strong accent is a problem. It isn't. I have colleagues from Brazil, India and Germany. What matters is being clear, being natural, and being yourself.

paras: It is often said that English opens doors, and in Brazil that is still largely true. Fluent speakers are believed to have an edge in many areas, from technology to finance, especially at multinational companies. But the way English is checked has changed. Today, many CVs are screened by software before a recruiter reads them, and a job posting that asks for advanced English usually means something very specific: you are expected to work in English, not just to read it.

That is why the line about English on a CV matters so much. Recruiters say that the word fluent is used far too often. A candidate who writes fluent is expected to hold a meeting, answer a question he did not prepare for and write a clear email. If he cannot, he rarely makes the shortlist. Many recruiters prefer an honest description: proficient in reading and writing, brushing up on speaking, for example, with a certificate or a track record to support it.

In the interview, soft skills are tested as much as grammar. Candidates are often asked to talk about a project, solve a problem or simply chat for a few minutes, and the conversation is watched as closely as the CV was read. A certificate can help you land a job interview, and a good cover letter in English can help too. But in the end, it is said, people hire people they can talk to.
